questionText: What does the idiom TO BITE THE BULLET mean?
options: A) To eat something hard
B) To endure a painful situation stoically
C) To shoot a gun
D) To make a rash decision
explanation: TO BITE THE BULLET means to endure a painful or difficult situation with courage. Originally, soldiers bit on a bullet during surgery to cope with pain.

questionText: Which proverb means that actions speak louder than words?
options: A) The pen is mightier than the sword.
B) Actions speak louder than words.
C) Practice what you preach.
D) A stitch in time saves nine.
explanation: ACTIONS SPEAK LOUDER THAN WORDS means what you do is more significant than what you say. It emphasizes deeds over promises.

questionText: What does the idiom TO BURN THE MIDNIGHT OIL mean?
options: A) To waste resources
B) To work late into the night
C) To start a fire
D) To cook at midnight
explanation: TO BURN THE MIDNIGHT OIL means to work or study late into the night — a reference to working by lamplight long after dark.

questionText: What does the proverb A PENNY SAVED IS A PENNY EARNED mean?
options: A) Money should be spent wisely
B) Saving money is as valuable as earning it
C) Wealth comes from earning
D) Pennies are not worth much
explanation: This proverb emphasizes the importance of thrift — saving money has the same practical value as earning it.

questionText: What does the idiom TO HAVE A CHIP ON ONE'S SHOULDER mean?
options: A) To have a physical injury
B) To carry snacks
C) To feel resentful about a past wrong
D) To be very proud
explanation: TO HAVE A CHIP ON ONE'S SHOULDER means to be easily offended because of a feeling that you have been treated unfairly in the past.

questionText: What does the idiom TO LET THE CAT OUT OF THE BAG mean?
options: A) To release a cat
B) To reveal a secret accidentally
C) To be careless
D) To open a closed container
explanation: TO LET THE CAT OUT OF THE BAG means to accidentally reveal information that was supposed to be kept secret.

questionText: What does the proverb STRIKE WHILE THE IRON IS HOT mean?
options: A) Work in hot conditions
B) Act quickly while opportunity exists
C) Hit hard when angry
D) Be a blacksmith
explanation: This proverb advises taking advantage of a favorable situation before the opportunity passes — from the practice of shaping hot metal quickly.

questionText: What does the idiom TO PULL SOMEONE'S LEG mean?
options: A) To physically pull someone
B) To tease or joke with someone
C) To help someone walk
D) To trip someone
explanation: TO PULL SOMEONE'S LEG means to tease, joke, or playfully deceive someone. It is not meant with malicious intent.

questionText: What does the proverb EVERY CLOUD HAS A SILVER LINING mean?
options: A) Clouds produce rain
B) Every difficult situation has some good aspect
C) Silver is hidden in clouds
D) Weather can be deceptive
explanation: This proverb encourages optimism — even in the worst situations, there is some element of good or hope.

questionText: What does the idiom TO BEAT AROUND THE BUSH mean?
options: A) To literally beat a bush
B) To avoid coming to the main point
C) To go around an obstacle
D) To work in a garden
explanation: TO BEAT AROUND THE BUSH means to talk about less important things to avoid the main topic, especially because it is embarrassing or difficult.

questionText: What does the idiom TO GO BACK TO THE DRAWING BOARD mean?
options: A) To return to school
B) To start a plan over from scratch
C) To draw a picture
D) To revisit an old project
explanation: TO GO BACK TO THE DRAWING BOARD means to start a plan or project over because the current approach has failed.

questionText: What does the proverb NECESSITY IS THE MOTHER OF INVENTION mean?
options: A) Mothers are creative
B) Need drives people to find solutions
C) Inventions are necessary
D) Mothers must be innovative
explanation: This proverb means that when people need something urgently, they are motivated to create or find a solution. Necessity drives invention.

questionText: What does the idiom ONCE IN A BLUE MOON mean?
options: A) During a lunar eclipse
B) Very rarely
C) Once a month
D) Every blue moon
explanation: ONCE IN A BLUE MOON means very rarely — a blue moon (the second full moon in a month) is an infrequent event.

questionText: What does the proverb THE GRASS IS ALWAYS GREENER ON THE OTHER SIDE mean?
options: A) Plants grow better elsewhere
B) People always want what others have
C) Nature is more beautiful far away
D) Agriculture is better in other countries
explanation: This proverb means that people tend to think others have better situations than they do, even when it is not true.

questionText: What does the idiom TO THROW IN THE TOWEL mean?
options: A) To clean up a mess
B) To give up or admit defeat
C) To throw a towel at someone
D) To start a fight
explanation: TO THROW IN THE TOWEL means to give up or admit that you are beaten — from boxing, where a trainer throws a towel into the ring to stop the fight.

questionText: What does the idiom TO HAVE A SKELETON IN THE CLOSET mean?
options: A) To have a morbid interest in death
B) To keep a scandalous secret
C) To collect bones
D) To have an old wardrobe
explanation: TO HAVE A SKELETON IN THE CLOSET means to have a shameful or embarrassing secret from the past that you want to keep hidden.

questionText: What does the proverb LOOK BEFORE YOU LEAP mean?
options: A) Always check the ground before jumping
B) Consider consequences before acting
C) Look both ways before crossing
D) Be physically cautious
explanation: LOOK BEFORE YOU LEAP advises considering consequences and potential risks carefully before taking action.

questionText: What does the idiom TO KILL TWO BIRDS WITH ONE STONE mean?
options: A) To be a hunter
B) To accomplish two things with one action
C) To throw a stone
D) To be efficient at hunting
explanation: TO KILL TWO BIRDS WITH ONE STONE means to accomplish two things with a single action — being highly efficient.

questionText: What does the proverb BIRDS OF A FEATHER FLOCK TOGETHER mean?
options: A) Birds live in groups
B) People with similar characters associate together
C) Feathers help birds fly together
D) Nature brings similar animals together
explanation: This proverb means that people tend to associate with others who have similar interests, beliefs, and values.

questionText: What does the idiom TO BITE THE HAND THAT FEEDS YOU mean?
options: A) To bite someone who gives you food
B) To act against those who help you
C) To be ungrateful about food
D) To be violent toward benefactors
explanation: TO BITE THE HAND THAT FEEDS YOU means to harm or act against those who support or help you — a metaphor for ingratitude.

questionText: What does the proverb A CHAIN IS ONLY AS STRONG AS ITS WEAKEST LINK mean?
options: A) Chains are important
B) A group is only as strong as its weakest member
C) Links in a chain can break
D) Teamwork requires strong chains
explanation: This proverb means the overall strength of a system depends on its most vulnerable component — one weak member can bring down the whole team.

questionText: What does the idiom TO SIT ON THE FENCE mean?
options: A) To physically rest on a fence
B) To avoid making a decision
C) To observe a situation
D) To be neutral and uninvolved
explanation: TO SIT ON THE FENCE means to avoid taking sides or making a decision — staying neutral rather than committing to a position.

questionText: What does the proverb IT TAKES TWO TO TANGO mean?
options: A) Dancing requires two people
B) Both parties are responsible in a conflict
C) Two people must always agree
D) Partnerships require two people
explanation: IT TAKES TWO TO TANGO means that both people in a situation share responsibility for it — neither party is entirely blameless.

questionText: What does the idiom TO ADD FUEL TO THE FIRE mean?
options: A) To keep a fire burning
B) To make a bad situation worse
C) To help solve a problem
D) To be a firefighter
explanation: TO ADD FUEL TO THE FIRE means to worsen an already bad situation by saying or doing something that provokes further conflict.

questionText: What does the proverb A LEOPARD CANNOT CHANGE ITS SPOTS mean?
options: A) Leopards are unchangeable animals
B) People cannot change their fundamental nature
C) Physical appearance is permanent
D) Animal patterns are fixed
explanation: This proverb means that a person cannot change their basic character or nature, even if they try.

questionText: What does the idiom TO STEAL SOMEONE'S THUNDER mean?
options: A) To steal something valuable
B) To take credit for or diminish someone else's achievement
C) To be louder than someone
D) To interrupt a storm
explanation: TO STEAL SOMEONE'S THUNDER means to take attention or credit away from someone else, diminishing their moment of recognition.

questionText: What does the proverb WHERE THERE IS A WILL THERE IS A WAY mean?
options: A) Determination leads to success
B) Wills are important legal documents
C) Roads lead to success
D) There is always an alternative
explanation: This proverb means that if you are determined enough to achieve something, you will find a way to do it.

questionText: What does the idiom A BLESSING IN DISGUISE mean?
options: A) A hidden blessing
B) Something that appears bad but turns out to be good
C) A blessing that is hidden
D) An unexpected gift
explanation: A BLESSING IN DISGUISE means something that seems unfortunate at first but results in something good — a misfortune with hidden benefits.

questionText: What does the proverb THE EARLY BIRD CATCHES THE WORM mean?
options: A) Birds wake early to find food
B) Being punctual and early leads to success
C) Arriving early is polite
D) Morning is the best time to work
explanation: THE EARLY BIRD CATCHES THE WORM means that those who start early or act promptly will have an advantage over those who do not.

questionText: What does the idiom TO CROSS THE RUBICON mean?
options: A) To cross a river
B) To make an irrevocable decision
C) To take a risk
D) To go on a journey
explanation: TO CROSS THE RUBICON means to take a decisive, irreversible step. It refers to Julius Caesar crossing the Rubicon River in 49 BC — an act of war from which there was no turning back.

questionText: What does the idiom THE LAST STRAW mean?
options: A) The final piece of hay
B) A small event that causes a reaction after many problems
C) An unimportant detail
D) The end of something
explanation: THE LAST STRAW (or the straw that broke the camel's back) means a minor issue that, coming on top of previous problems, makes the situation unbearable.

questionText: What does the proverb TOO MANY COOKS SPOIL THE BROTH mean?
options: A) Cooking with many people is difficult
B) Too many people involved in something make it worse
C) Cooks are inefficient in groups
D) Food tastes better when made alone
explanation: TOO MANY COOKS SPOIL THE BROTH means that when too many people are involved in managing something, it becomes disorganized and the result suffers.

questionText: What does the idiom TO HAVE YOUR CAKE AND EAT IT TOO mean?
options: A) To be greedy with food
B) To want to benefit from two conflicting options simultaneously
C) To enjoy having cake
D) To save and eat simultaneously
explanation: TO HAVE YOUR CAKE AND EAT IT TOO means to want to enjoy two things that are mutually exclusive — you cannot keep your cake if you eat it.

questionText: What does the proverb GIVE A MAN A FISH AND YOU FEED HIM FOR A DAY mean in context?
options: A) Fishing is a useful skill
B) Giving resources is better than teaching skills
C) Teaching skills provides lasting benefits over short-term handouts
D) Food should be shared freely
explanation: The full proverb is: Give a man a fish... teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime. It advocates for education and empowerment over temporary relief.

questionText: What does the idiom TO WEATHER THE STORM mean?
options: A) To survive in bad weather
B) To endure a difficult period
C) To predict the weather
D) To be a sailor
explanation: TO WEATHER THE STORM means to survive a difficult period or situation, especially without being badly harmed.

questionText: What does the proverb ACTIONS SPEAK LOUDER THAN WORDS mean in formal usage?
options: A) Noise is more powerful than speech
B) What people do is more meaningful than what they say
C) Actions are more impressive
D) Words cannot be trusted
explanation: This proverb emphasizes that behavior and deeds are a more reliable indicator of true intentions and character than mere words or promises.

questionText: What does the idiom BARKING UP THE WRONG TREE mean?
options: A) A dog is confused
B) Pursuing a mistaken line of thought or action
C) To make a wrong accusation
D) To be in the wrong place
explanation: BARKING UP THE WRONG TREE means pursuing a mistaken or misguided course of action — like a dog barking at a tree where its quarry is no longer present.

questionText: What does the proverb CURIOSITY KILLED THE CAT mean?
options: A) Cats are curious animals
B) Being too inquisitive can lead to trouble
C) Curiosity is dangerous for animals
D) Questions can be fatal
explanation: CURIOSITY KILLED THE CAT is a warning that being too curious can get you into trouble or cause harm.

questionText: What does the idiom TO PUT ALL EGGS IN ONE BASKET mean?
options: A) To be careless with eggs
B) To risk everything on a single venture
C) To concentrate resources carefully
D) To store things safely
explanation: TO PUT ALL EGGS IN ONE BASKET means to concentrate all your resources, hopes, or efforts on one thing — increasing the risk of total loss if it fails.

questionText: What does the proverb EMPTY VESSELS MAKE THE MOST NOISE mean?
options: A) Empty containers produce echoes
B) Those with least knowledge are most talkative
C) Quiet people are most knowledgeable
D) Noise is associated with emptiness
explanation: This proverb means that people who know the least are often the loudest — shallow people tend to speak the most.

questionText: What does the idiom TO BE ON CLOUD NINE mean?
options: A) To be in an airplane
B) To be extremely happy
C) To daydream
D) To float above problems
explanation: TO BE ON CLOUD NINE means to be extremely happy and elated — in a state of perfect happiness or bliss.

questionText: What does the proverb WELL BEGUN IS HALF DONE mean?
options: A) Starting is the hardest part
B) A good start makes the rest of the task easier
C) The beginning determines the end
D) Half the work is done at the start
explanation: WELL BEGUN IS HALF DONE means that a proper start makes the entire task easier to complete. A good beginning sets the tone for success.

questionText: What does the idiom TO JUMP ON THE BANDWAGON mean?
options: A) To join a music group
B) To follow a popular trend or movement
C) To board a vehicle suddenly
D) To be enthusiastic about music
explanation: TO JUMP ON THE BANDWAGON means to adopt a popular activity or opinion, often without careful thought, because many others are doing it.

questionText: What does the proverb HONESTY IS THE BEST POLICY mean?
options: A) Honesty is a legal requirement
B) Being truthful is the best approach in all situations
C) Policies should be honest
D) Truth is always convenient
explanation: HONESTY IS THE BEST POLICY means that being truthful, even when it is difficult, is always the most beneficial approach in the long run.

questionText: What does the idiom TO MAKE A MOUNTAIN OUT OF A MOLEHILL mean?
options: A) To build terrain features
B) To exaggerate a minor problem
C) To ignore a problem
D) To be a geologist
explanation: TO MAKE A MOUNTAIN OUT OF A MOLEHILL means to exaggerate the importance or difficulty of a minor problem — turning something small into something large.

questionText: What does the proverb THE PROOF OF THE PUDDING IS IN THE EATING mean?
options: A) Pudding must be tasted to be judged
B) The true value of something can only be judged by trying it
C) Actions speak louder than recipes
D) Food must be tested before serving
explanation: This proverb means that the real quality or truth of something can only be assessed through direct experience or use — not by appearance or description.

questionText: What does the idiom TO HAVE THE LAST LAUGH mean?
options: A) To be the funniest person
B) To ultimately succeed after seeming to be at a disadvantage
C) To laugh at the end of a joke
D) To be the last to understand
explanation: TO HAVE THE LAST LAUGH means to ultimately succeed or prove others wrong after initially seeming defeated or ridiculed.

questionText: What does the proverb TIME AND TIDE WAIT FOR NO MAN mean?
options: A) Tides are unpredictable
B) Opportunities and time do not pause for anyone
C) Nature is indifferent to human needs
D) Sailors must be on time
explanation: TIME AND TIDE WAIT FOR NO MAN means that time and opportunity will not stop or slow down for you — you must act promptly.

questionText: What does the idiom TO THROW CAUTION TO THE WIND mean?
options: A) To be reckless with safety equipment
B) To take risks without worrying about consequences
C) To disregard weather warnings
D) To be a daring outdoor adventurer
explanation: TO THROW CAUTION TO THE WIND means to act recklessly, ignoring risks — abandoning all concern for safety or prudence.

questionText: What does the proverb JACK OF ALL TRADES, MASTER OF NONE mean?
options: A) Versatility is always a weakness
B) Someone with many skills but not expert at any one
C) A person named Jack is generalist
D) Having many interests is foolish
explanation: JACK OF ALL TRADES, MASTER OF NONE describes someone competent in many areas but not outstanding in any. The full proverb sometimes adds: though often better than a master of one.
